question: Under the assimilated EU drivers' hours rules, what is the normal maximum daily driving time?
explanation: Daily driving is limited to 9 hours. It can be extended to 10 hours, but only twice in a week.

question: Under the EU drivers' hours rules, how many times a week may you extend daily driving to 10 hours?
explanation: The 9-hour daily limit may be extended to 10 hours no more than twice in a fixed week.

question: What is the most you may drive in a single week under the EU drivers' hours rules?
explanation: Weekly driving is capped at 56 hours. The 48 and 60 hour figures are working time limits, not driving limits.

question: What is the most you may drive in any two consecutive weeks under the EU rules?
explanation: You may drive no more than 90 hours in any two consecutive weeks, so two 56-hour weeks in a row are not allowed.

question: Under the EU rules, after how much driving must you take a break of at least 45 minutes?
explanation: A break or breaks totalling at least 45 minutes must be taken after no more than 4 hours 30 minutes of driving.

question: You want to split your 45-minute break. Which split do the EU rules allow?
explanation: The break can be split into at least 15 minutes followed by at least 30 minutes. The order matters: the longer part comes second.

question: Does a 10-minute stop count towards your 45-minute break under the EU rules?
optionB: Only if you leave the cab
explanation: Breaks of less than 15 minutes do not count towards the required break, however many you take.

question: How long is a regular daily rest period under the EU drivers' hours rules?
explanation: A regular daily rest is at least 11 hours. It can be reduced to 9 hours a limited number of times.

question: What is the shortest a reduced daily rest may be under the EU rules?
explanation: A daily rest may be reduced to no less than 9 continuous hours, with no compensation needed.

question: How many reduced daily rests may you take between two weekly rest periods?
explanation: You may reduce your daily rest to 9 hours no more than three times between any two weekly rest periods.

question: You split your regular daily rest into two parts. Which split is allowed?
explanation: A split daily rest is at least 3 hours followed by at least 9 hours, 12 hours in total. The 9-hour part must come last.

question: How long is a regular weekly rest period under the EU rules?
explanation: A regular weekly rest is at least 45 continuous hours. A reduced weekly rest is at least 24 hours.

question: What is the shortest a reduced weekly rest may be?
explanation: A reduced weekly rest is at least 24 hours but less than 45, and the reduction must be made up later.

question: A weekly rest must start no later than the end of how many consecutive 24-hour periods?
explanation: Weekly rest must be taken after no more than six consecutive 24-hour periods from the end of the last weekly rest. Twelve applies only to some international coach trips.

question: You took a reduced weekly rest. By when must you make up the hours you missed?
optionA: Before the end of the same week
optionB: By the end of the following week
optionC: By the end of the third week after
optionD: By the end of the fourth month after
explanation: The reduction must be compensated by an equivalent rest, taken in one block, before the end of the third week following the week in question.

question: Under the GB domestic drivers' hours rules, what is the daily driving limit for goods vehicles?
explanation: The GB domestic rules allow up to 10 hours of driving in a day. The 9-hour figure belongs to the EU rules.

question: Under the GB domestic rules, what is the daily duty limit for a goods vehicle driver?
explanation: Goods vehicle drivers on GB domestic rules may be on duty for no more than 11 hours in a working day on which they drive.

question: With two drivers on board (multi-manning), each must take a 9-hour daily rest within what period?
explanation: When multi-manning, each driver must have a daily rest of at least 9 consecutive hours within 30 hours of the end of the last rest.

question: You take your regular daily rest on a ferry. How may it be interrupted?
optionB: Three times, totalling no more than 1 hour
optionC: Twice, totalling no more than 1 hour
explanation: A regular daily rest on a ferry or train may be interrupted no more than twice, for no more than 1 hour in total, for example to drive on or off.

question: You are told you will wait 2 hours at a depot before you can unload. How do you record this time?
explanation: Waiting time whose length is known in advance is recorded as availability. It is not a break or rest.

question: You spend an hour loading your lorry at the depot. Which tachograph mode should you use?
explanation: Loading is work other than driving, so it is recorded as other work.

question: Which time do digital and smart tachographs record in?
explanation: Digital and smart tachographs record UTC, which is one hour behind British Summer Time, so allow for the difference when making manual entries in summer.

question: Your driver card is stolen. Within how long must you report it and apply for a new one?
explanation: You must report a lost, stolen or faulty card to DVLA and apply for a replacement within seven calendar days.

question: While waiting for a replacement driver card, for how long may you keep driving?
explanation: You may drive without your card for a maximum of 15 calendar days while you wait for the replacement.

question: You are driving without your driver card while a new one is made. What must you do each day?
optionA: Take printouts at the start and end
optionB: Carry a signed note from your operator
optionD: Fill in an analogue chart instead
explanation: You must take two printouts, at the start and end of the day, and write your details on them so the day is recorded.

question: How many tachograph driver cards may you hold?
explanation: A driver may hold only one driver card and must never use anyone else's.

question: On a domestic journey, which tachograph records must you be able to show an examiner?
explanation: For domestic or AETR journeys you must produce records for the current day and the previous 28 calendar days.

question: How often must an operator download the data from each driver card?
explanation: Driver cards must be downloaded at least every 28 days. The 90-day interval is for the vehicle unit.

question: What is the longest period a single analogue tachograph chart may cover?
explanation: A chart must not be used to cover a period longer than 24 hours, so carry enough spare charts for the journey.

question: Under the road transport working time rules, what is the most you may work on average each week?
explanation: Working time must not exceed an average of 48 hours a week, normally over 17 weeks. Up to 60 hours is allowed in a single week.

question: Under the working time rules, how long may you work before you must take a break?
explanation: You must not work more than 6 consecutive hours without a break. The 4 hours 30 minutes figure is the driving limit before a break.

question: You feel sleepy while driving on a motorway. What should you do?
optionA: Open a window and keep driving
optionB: Stop on the hard shoulder to rest
optionC: Turn the radio up and carry on
optionD: Leave at the next exit and rest
explanation: Leave the motorway at the next exit or services and rest. The Highway Code suggests two cups of caffeinated coffee and a rest of at least 15 minutes.

question: Your doctor says you have sleep apnoea causing excessive sleepiness. What must you do?
explanation: Lorry drivers must tell the DVLA about a condition such as obstructive sleep apnoea that causes excessive sleepiness.

question: What is the minimum eyesight standard in your better eye for a lorry licence?
explanation: Lorry and bus drivers need at least 0.8 (6/7.5) in the better eye and at least 0.1 (6/60) in the other.

question: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, what is the drink-drive breath limit?
explanation: The breath limit is 35 micrograms of alcohol per 100 ml of breath. The 80 figure is the blood limit, in milligrammes.

question: What is the drink-drive blood alcohol limit in Scotland?
explanation: Scotland's limit is 50 milligrammes per 100 ml of blood, lower than the 80 used in the rest of the UK.

question: What is the minimum legal tread depth for lorry tyres, across three-quarters of the tread width?
explanation: Large vehicles need at least 1 mm across three-quarters of the tread width in a continuous band. The 1.6 mm figure is for cars and light vans.

question: Tyres more than 10 years old must not be fitted to which axles of a lorry over 3.5 tonnes?
explanation: Tyres over 10 years old must not be used on the front (steering) axles of goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes, where a failure is most dangerous.

question: When should you check your tyre pressures?
optionD: At the end of each shift
explanation: Check pressures when the tyres are cold. Warm tyres give a misleadingly high reading.

question: When should you carry out your walkaround check?
optionB: Only after a breakdown or repair
explanation: A daily walkaround check before you start is the driver's responsibility, as DVSA recommends for all commercial vehicles.

question: Your walkaround check finds a damaged brake air hose. What should you do?
optionA: Report it and do not drive
optionB: Drive slowly back to the depot
optionC: Note it for the next service
optionD: Tape it and use low gears
explanation: A brake defect makes the vehicle unroadworthy. Report it and do not drive until it has been repaired.

question: Before moving off, the low air pressure warning is still showing. What should you do?
optionA: Pump the brake pedal to clear it
optionB: Wait until the warning goes out
optionC: Drive gently to build up air
optionD: Move off on the parking brake
explanation: The warning means there is not enough air for the brakes to work properly. Wait for the pressure to build and the warning to go out.

question: Why should you drain the air tanks regularly, especially in cold weather?
optionA: To release excess pressure from them
optionB: To top up the brake fluid
optionC: To remove water that could freeze
explanation: Moisture collects in air tanks and can freeze in valves and pipes, causing brake failure. Automatic drain valves still need checking.

question: Why might the brakes fade on a long downhill stretch?
optionA: The air pressure gets too high
optionC: The brake linings get too cold
explanation: Continuous use of the footbrake overheats the brakes and they lose effectiveness, which is brake fade.

question: How can you avoid brake fade on a long, steep descent?
optionA: Use a low gear and the endurance brake
optionB: Coast down in neutral to save fuel
optionC: Hold the footbrake on all the way down
optionD: Use the parking brake to slow down
explanation: Select a low gear before the descent and use the endurance brake (retarder) so the service brakes stay cool for when you need them.

question: What is an endurance braking system (retarder) designed to do?
optionA: Stop the wheels locking when you brake
optionD: Work only in an emergency stop
explanation: A retarder helps hold the vehicle's speed, mainly on descents, so the service brakes are not overused. ABS is what stops wheels locking.

question: How should you use an endurance brake on an icy road?
optionA: Fully on, to save the service brakes
optionB: Only when the trailer is loaded
optionC: With care; it can lock the wheels
optionD: Exactly as you would on a dry road
explanation: On slippery roads a retarder can lock the drive wheels and cause a skid. Use it with care, or switch it off if the maker advises.

question: The ABS warning light stays on after you move off. What does this mean?
optionA: The parking brake is still on
optionD: There is a fault in the ABS
explanation: The light should go out once you move off. If it stays on, the ABS has a fault and needs checking; the brakes still work but without anti-lock.

question: You must stop quickly in a lorry fitted with ABS. How should you brake?
explanation: With ABS, apply the brake firmly and keep the pressure on. The system prevents the wheels locking, so do not pump the pedal.

question: The air pressure gauge drops sharply while you are driving. What should you do?
optionB: Stop as soon as it is safe
optionD: Speed up to recharge the air
explanation: Falling air pressure means the brakes may soon fail. Stop safely as soon as you can and get the fault seen to.

question: Before reversing under a semi-trailer to couple up, what should you check?
explanation: The trailer parking brake must be applied so the trailer cannot roll away as the unit reverses under it.

question: After coupling, how can you check that the fifth wheel jaws have locked?
optionA: Rock the trailer from side to side
explanation: A gentle pull forward with the trailer brake applied (a tug test) shows whether the kingpin is locked, as well as checking the locking handle visually.

question: Why must the ground be firm and level before you uncouple a semi-trailer?
optionD: The fifth wheel will not open
explanation: On soft or sloping ground the landing legs can sink or the trailer can tip as the unit pulls away.

question: On most trailers, what does the red air line coupling supply?
explanation: The red coupling is the emergency or supply line and the yellow is the service or control line. Connecting them the wrong way round affects the trailer brakes.

question: The power steering fails while you are driving. What will you notice?
optionB: The lorry pulls hard to the left
explanation: Without power assistance the steering still works but needs far more effort, so slow down and stop safely.

question: Why must you make sure the fuel cap is secure after filling up?
optionA: The fuel gauge may stop working
optionB: Diesel evaporates quickly in the sun
explanation: Diesel spilt on the road is very slippery, especially for motorcyclists. Check the cap and seal and that tanks are not overfilled.

question: When checking the engine oil level, where should the lorry be?
explanation: Check the oil on level ground with the engine switched off, or the dipstick reading will be wrong.

question: The oil pressure warning light comes on while you are driving. What should you do?
optionA: Keep going to the next services
explanation: Low oil pressure can wreck the engine within minutes. Stop as soon as it is safe and switch the engine off.

question: What are wheel nut indicators for?
optionC: Showing if a wheel nut has moved
explanation: The pointers line up when fitted, so a pointer out of line shows at a glance that a nut has loosened.

question: What is spray-suppression equipment on a lorry for?
explanation: Spray suppression on the wheel arches cuts the spray that would blind drivers behind and beside you on wet roads.

question: You raised the air suspension to load at a bay. What must you do before driving away?
optionA: Return it to normal ride height
optionB: Raise it higher for more clearance
optionD: Lower it fully onto the stops
explanation: Driving at the wrong ride height affects handling, braking and stability, so reset the suspension before you move off.

question: Before you tilt the cab, what should you do?
optionA: Start the engine to build air
optionB: Secure any loose items in it
explanation: Loose items will fall forward and can break the windscreen. Also make sure the area in front of the cab is clear.

question: What is the main cause of a lorry skidding?
explanation: Skids are caused by the driver: too fast for the conditions, harsh braking, accelerating or steering. Conditions only make it more likely.

question: What is most likely to make an articulated lorry jack-knife?
optionA: Driving too slowly up a steep hill
optionB: A light load spread along the trailer
optionC: Using the retarder on a dry road
optionD: Harsh braking, especially on a bend
explanation: Braking hard, especially while turning, can lock the wheels so the trailer swings round and pushes the unit sideways.

question: The engine coolant warning light comes on. What should you avoid doing?
optionB: Stopping in a safe place soon
explanation: Removing the cap while the system is hot can spray scalding coolant. Stop, switch off and wait for it to cool.

question: A front tyre bursts while you are driving. What should you do?
optionA: Brake hard to stop as fast as possible
optionB: Hold the wheel firmly, slow gently
explanation: Grip the wheel firmly, keep straight and let the lorry slow gradually before braking gently and stopping safely.

question: Your trailer's air lines are connected. What should you check before moving off?
explanation: Test that the trailer brakes respond before moving off. The landing legs must be fully raised, not down.

question: What does a load-sensing valve on a lorry's braking system do?
optionA: Warns that the lorry is overweight
optionD: Adjusts braking force to the load
explanation: A load-sensing valve matches braking force to the weight on the axle, so an empty vehicle does not lock its wheels.

question: A load restraint system must be able to hold what force in the forward direction?
optionA: The full weight of the load
optionB: Half the weight of the load
optionC: A quarter of the load's weight
optionD: Twice the weight of the load
explanation: DVSA's performance standard is the full load weight forwards, and half the load weight sideways and rearwards, for normal driving.

question: A load restraint system must be able to hold what force to each side?
optionA: The full weight of the load
optionB: Half the weight of the load
optionC: A quarter of the load's weight
optionD: Twice the weight of the load
explanation: Sideways and rearwards, the restraint must hold at least half the load's weight. Forwards it must hold the full weight.

question: A load restraint system must be able to hold what force towards the rear?
optionA: The full weight of the load
optionB: Twice the weight of the load
optionC: Half the weight of the load
explanation: Rearwards the standard is half the load's weight, the same as to each side. Loads move backwards when you accelerate or climb.

question: What is a sheet or cover over a load mainly for?
optionA: Restraining the load in an emergency stop
optionC: Holding the load against the headboard
optionD: Containing the load, not restraining it
explanation: Covers stop items bouncing out or loose material blowing away. They do not restrain a load, so use lashings or other restraint as well.

question: Why can't you rely on a heavy load's own weight to keep it in place?
optionA: Friction alone is too low to hold it
optionB: Heavy loads only ever move on sharp bends
explanation: Friction between most loads and the load bed is low, so a load will slide once the vehicle brakes, turns or accelerates unless it is secured.

question: Where should a load's centre of gravity be?
optionB: Low and near the centre line
optionC: Low and against one side wall
optionD: High and over the rear axle
explanation: Keeping the weight low and central keeps both the load and the vehicle stable, especially on bends and roundabouts.

question: You deliver part of your load. Why might an axle now be overloaded?
optionA: The total weight has gone up
optionB: The tyres have lost some of their pressure
explanation: Removing part of a load lowers the gross weight but can shift more weight onto one axle. This is the diminishing load effect.

question: You notice your load has shifted but is still on the lorry. What should you do?
optionA: Carry on and fix it when you reach your drop
optionB: Brake firmly to push it forward again
optionC: Speed up to reach the depot sooner
optionD: Slow down and stop safely to re-secure it
explanation: Slow down, avoid harsh braking or steering and stop somewhere safe. You must not continue until the load is secure.

question: Part of your load falls onto a motorway. What should you do?
optionC: Drive on and tell your operator
explanation: Stop as soon as it is safe and call 999 to report it. Do not try to retrieve anything from a motorway or dual carriageway.

question: At your delivery point the load has become unstable. What should happen?
optionA: You drive it back to the depot
optionC: You release the straps to settle it
optionD: You unload it by hand at once
explanation: Keep the vehicle on site until a safe unloading plan is agreed. A vehicle with a known unstable load must not go back on the road.

question: A load on your flatbed is leaning to one side. What must you not do?
optionA: Set up an exclusion zone around the lorry
optionB: Call for trained help to unload it
optionC: Release the lashings before it is stable
explanation: Releasing lashings on a leaning load can bring it down on you. Never walk under it; make the area safe and get competent help.

question: Who is responsible for making sure a load is secure?
explanation: Drivers and operators must choose a suitable securing system and check it. The driver is responsible for the vehicle on the road.

question: What is the standard maximum length of an articulated lorry with an ordinary semi-trailer?
explanation: The standard limit for an articulated vehicle is 16.5 metres. Longer semi-trailer combinations (up to 18.55 metres) have their own rules, and 18.75 metres is the drawbar (lorry and trailer) limit.

question: What is the maximum length of a rigid lorry towing a drawbar trailer?
explanation: A drawbar combination (road train) may be up to 18.75 metres long, longer than the 16.5-metre limit for articulated lorries.

question: What is the general maximum width of a goods vehicle?
explanation: Most goods vehicles may be up to 2.55 metres wide. Refrigerated vehicles may be 2.6 metres because of their thicker insulated walls.

question: What is the maximum width of a refrigerated lorry with insulated walls?
explanation: Refrigerated vehicles are allowed 2.6 metres, slightly more than the 2.55-metre general limit.

question: What is the usual maximum gross weight of a six-axle articulated lorry?
explanation: A six-axle articulated lorry meeting the axle and suspension rules may operate at up to 44 tonnes.

question: Above what travelling height must a notice in the cab show your vehicle's height?
explanation: If the vehicle's overall travelling height is over 3 metres, the height must be shown in feet and inches on a notice the driver can see.

question: Why should you know your vehicle's height in feet and inches as well as metres?
optionA: The law uses only feet and inches
optionB: Satnavs only use feet and inches
optionC: Some bridge signs show only feet
explanation: Older bridge and headroom signs may show only imperial heights, so you need both to be sure you will clear the bridge.

question: Your lorry hits a railway bridge. Who must you tell straight away?
optionA: Your operator, at the end of shift
optionC: The council, by letter or email
optionD: The railway, by the number on it
explanation: A bridge strike can make the line unsafe for trains. Call the number on the bridge identification plate at once, and 999 if anyone is in danger.

question: Where can you find your vehicle's maximum permitted axle weights?
explanation: The plate fitted in the cab (the ministry plate) gives the gross and axle weights the vehicle may run at in Great Britain.

question: What is a likely effect of overloading a lorry?
explanation: Extra weight makes the brakes work harder and lengthens stopping distances. It also strains the tyres and suspension.

question: Why must a loose load such as sand or gravel be sheeted?
optionA: To keep its weight within limits
optionC: To stop it blowing onto the road
explanation: Loose material blown or spilt from a lorry can hit other road users and their windscreens, so it must be contained.

question: Which lorry is most affected by a strong crosswind?
explanation: High sides catch the wind and an empty vehicle has little weight to resist it, so it is the most likely to be blown off course or over.

question: Why is a part-filled tanker without baffles harder to control?
optionA: The liquid surges when you brake
optionB: It weighs more than a full tank
optionC: Its brakes are much less effective
optionD: Its centre of gravity is lower
explanation: Liquid moves forward and back in a part-filled tank, pushing the vehicle on as you brake. Brake early and smoothly.

question: How does a high load affect a lorry on bends?
optionA: It grips the road better on bends
optionB: It is more likely to roll over
explanation: A high load raises the centre of gravity, so the vehicle can roll over at a lower speed on bends and roundabouts.

question: How should a container be secured on a skeletal trailer?
optionB: With one ratchet strap over the top
optionC: With all the twist locks engaged
explanation: Every twist lock must be engaged and locked before moving. A container's weight will not keep it on the trailer.

question: A ratchet strap has a cut in its webbing. What should you do?
optionA: Use it only for light loads now
optionB: Tie a knot over the damage
optionC: Tape it and keep using it
optionD: Replace it before you use it
explanation: Damaged webbing can fail under load. Take it out of use; knots and tape weaken it further.

question: What is a headboard on a flatbed lorry for?
optionA: Stopping the load hitting the cab
optionC: Reducing the wind resistance at speed
explanation: A headboard protects the driver if the load moves forward, but it is not a substitute for lashing the load.

question: A lorry is plated at 18,000 kg gross and weighs 7,500 kg unladen. What is its maximum payload?
explanation: Payload is the gross weight minus the unladen weight: 18,000 minus 7,500 is 10,500 kg.

question: When loading mixed goods, where should the heaviest items go?
optionC: At the bottom, near the centre
optionD: Against one side wall, near the doors
explanation: Heavy items low and central keep the centre of gravity down and spread the weight across the axles.

question: Before loading, what should you check on the load platform?
explanation: Check the platform, bodywork, anchorage points and twist locks are sound before the load goes on.

question: In England and Wales, what is the speed limit for a lorry over 7.5 tonnes on a single carriageway?
explanation: Goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes are limited to 50 mph on single carriageways in England and Wales, unless signs show lower. In Scotland it is 40 mph.

question: In England and Wales, what is the speed limit for a lorry over 7.5 tonnes on a dual carriageway?
explanation: The dual carriageway limit for these lorries in England and Wales is 60 mph; in Scotland it is 50 mph.

question: What is the motorway speed limit for a goods vehicle over 7.5 tonnes?
explanation: The motorway limit is 60 mph, although the speed limiter will usually hold the lorry to about 56 mph.

question: In Scotland, what is the speed limit for a lorry over 7.5 tonnes on a single carriageway?
explanation: Scotland kept a 40 mph single carriageway limit for goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes; England and Wales use 50 mph.

question: In Scotland, what is the speed limit for a lorry over 7.5 tonnes on a dual carriageway?
explanation: On Scottish dual carriageways these lorries are limited to 50 mph, 10 mph less than in England and Wales.

question: A goods vehicle over 3.5 tonnes must have a speed limiter set to what speed?
explanation: Speed limiters on goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes are set at 90 km/h, about 56 mph.

question: On a motorway with three or more lanes, which lane must a lorry over 7.5 tonnes not use?
explanation: Goods vehicles over 7.5 tonnes must not use the right-hand lane of a motorway with three or more lanes, except in prescribed circumstances such as roadworks.

question: What is the least room the Highway Code says to give a cyclist when overtaking at up to 30 mph?
explanation: Leave at least 1.5 metres at speeds up to 30 mph, and more at higher speeds. A lorry's draught can unsettle a cyclist.

question: When passing a horse rider, what is the most speed the Highway Code advises?
explanation: Pass horses at under 10 mph, leaving at least 2 metres, and do not rev the engine or use air brakes noisily close by.

question: Under the Highway Code hierarchy, who has the greatest responsibility to reduce danger?
optionB: Those who can cause most harm
optionD: Those travelling at the lowest speed
explanation: Those who can cause the greatest harm have the greatest responsibility, which puts lorry drivers near the top of the hierarchy.

question: At traffic lights with an advanced stop line for cyclists, where should a lorry stop?
optionA: Right up to the first white line
optionC: Well back from the first white line
optionD: Just over the first line, in the box
explanation: The Highway Code says drivers of large vehicles should stop far enough behind the first white line to see the whole cyclists' area, allowing for the blind spot in front of the cab.

question: Why must you check your nearside mirrors before and during a left turn?
optionA: To check the load is secure
explanation: Cyclists and motorcyclists can come up on your nearside, and the trailer's rear wheels cut in on the turn, so keep checking.

question: You are turning left and a cyclist is going straight ahead on your nearside. What should you do?
optionA: Wait and let them go first
optionB: Turn first, as you are larger
optionD: Turn slowly in front of them
explanation: You should not cut across cyclists going ahead when turning. Hold back until they have passed the junction.

question: When turning left into a narrow road, why may you need to keep well out?
optionA: To stop the load sliding off the bed
optionB: Your rear wheels cut in on the turn
optionC: To give oncoming traffic more room
explanation: A long vehicle's rear wheels follow a tighter line than the front, so you may need to keep out and watch for anything coming up on the nearside.

question: Your lorry cannot pass round the centre of a mini-roundabout. What may you do?
optionB: Go round it the wrong way
optionD: Stop and wait for the road to clear
explanation: All vehicles should pass round the central markings except large vehicles that physically cannot. Then take care and drive over them.

question: On a roundabout, why may a long vehicle need to straddle lanes?
optionB: To save fuel on the bend
optionD: To get the vehicle round safely
explanation: Long vehicles may need to take a different course or straddle lanes to get round. Signal clearly and watch for others alongside.

question: How should you change your following gap in wet weather?
explanation: Stopping distances at least double on wet roads, so at least double your gap.

question: On icy roads, stopping distances can increase by up to how much?
explanation: On ice, stopping distances can be up to ten times those on a dry road, so slow down and leave a much bigger gap.

question: What gap does the Highway Code advise for a large vehicle in a tunnel?
explanation: Large vehicles should keep a four-second gap in tunnels; in a queue in a tunnel leave at least 5 metres.

question: You cannot see behind the lorry to reverse. What should you do?
explanation: Use a reliable person to guide you, or get out and look. A reversing alarm warns others but does not show you what is behind.

question: What does a front (class VI) mirror let you see?
optionA: The area just in front of the cab
optionB: Traffic far behind the trailer's rear
optionD: The trailer wheels on a bend
explanation: Cab-forward lorries have a blind spot directly in front of the cab, where a pedestrian or cyclist can be hidden. The front mirror covers it.

question: What does a close-proximity (class V) mirror let you see?
optionB: The area beside the passenger door
optionC: The roof of the trailer and load
optionD: The traffic in the right-hand lanes
explanation: The close-proximity mirror shows the area alongside the nearside of the cab, where a cyclist can be hidden from the main mirrors.

question: You are stopped at a crossing with pedestrians nearby. What should you check before moving off?
optionA: The trailer parking brake is released
optionC: Nobody is just in front of the cab
explanation: Pedestrians, especially children, may be close to the front of the cab and out of sight. Check the front mirror before moving off.

question: Your lorry is only slightly faster than one ahead on a dual carriageway. What should you do?
optionB: Flash them to pull over and let you by
optionD: Only pass if you can do it quickly
explanation: A long, slow overtake holds up traffic behind. Only overtake if you can do it quickly and safely.

question: You are about to pass a cyclist in strong crosswinds. What should you do?
optionC: Sound the horn as you pass
explanation: Wind and the draught from your lorry can push a cyclist off course, so give more room than usual.

question: Why should you keep well back when following another large vehicle?
explanation: Large vehicles block your view. Dropping back lets you see and plan ahead, and lets the driver see you in their mirrors.

question: A sign at a level crossing tells you to phone for permission to cross. What must you do?
optionA: Open the gates and cross quickly
optionD: Wait for a train to pass first
explanation: You must obey a sign telling you to use the railway telephone. Large and slow vehicles take longer to cross, so a train could arrive first.

question: In fog, when must you use headlights?
optionA: When you can't see beyond 200 metres
optionB: When you can't see beyond 50 metres
optionD: When you can't see beyond 100 metres
explanation: You must use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you cannot see more than 100 metres.

question: You are turning into a side road and a pedestrian is waiting to cross it. What should you do?
optionC: Sound the horn to warn them
optionD: Wave them across the main road
explanation: At a junction you should give way to pedestrians crossing or waiting to cross the road you are turning into.

question: Why is a motorcyclist hard to spot from a lorry cab?
optionA: They always ride in the gutter
optionB: They are narrow and easily hidden
optionC: They are always slower than lorries
explanation: Motorcyclists are narrow and can approach fast or sit in a blind spot. Check mirrors carefully before changing lanes or turning.

question: What is the safest way to plan a route for a large lorry?
optionC: Use a lorry satnav or route map
optionD: Follow the lorry in front of you
explanation: Car satnavs can send lorries under low bridges and down unsuitable roads. Use a lorry-specific system or plan the route in advance.

question: You are driving behind a cyclist on a narrow road. Why may they ride in the centre of the lane?
optionA: To stop you overtaking at all
optionD: To be seen and stay safe
explanation: Cyclists may ride in the centre of the lane on narrow or quiet roads for their own safety. Wait until you can pass with enough room.

question: How much periodic training must you complete to keep your Driver CPC?
explanation: Professional lorry drivers must do 35 hours of Driver CPC periodic training in each 5-year period.

question: Your 35 hours of periodic training include a National course. What can't you then do?
optionD: Renew your Driver CPC at all
explanation: Including any National course gives you a National Driver CPC, which is valid in the UK but not for professional driving in Europe.

question: Which of these drivers is exempt from needing a Driver CPC?
optionA: A driver doing short local deliveries
optionB: A driver on a part-time contract
optionC: A driver of a lorry limited to 28 mph
optionD: A driver who only works nights
explanation: Exemptions include vehicles limited to 28 mph, armed forces and police vehicles, personal use, and driving that is not the main part of your job.

question: Where must a goods vehicle's operator's licence identity disc be displayed?
explanation: Each vehicle used under an operator's licence must show a valid identity disc in its windscreen, where enforcement officers can see it.

question: You move to a new home address. Who must you tell so your driving licence can be updated?
explanation: You must tell the DVLA when you change address so your licence can be updated. Driving with the wrong address on your licence can lead to a fine of up to £1,000.

question: Once you reach 65, how often must you renew your lorry licence entitlement?
explanation: Lorry and bus entitlement is renewed every 5 years, and every year from age 65, with a medical report.

question: Which form is used for the medical report needed for a lorry licence?
explanation: The D4 medical examination report is completed by a doctor or optician for lorry and bus licences. D2 is the application form itself.

question: What does a business need before it can use goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes for its work?
explanation: Goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes used in connection with a business need an operator's licence (an O licence) from the Traffic Commissioner.

question: When is a new lorry's first annual test due?
explanation: Goods vehicles over 3.5 tonnes need an annual test from one year after first registration, unlike cars, which wait three years.

question: What do you carry as proof of your Driver CPC?
explanation: The driver qualification card (Driver CPC card) is proof of your Driver CPC and must be carried when driving professionally.

question: You are leaving your lorry. What should you do before getting out of the cab?
optionA: Leave the engine running for the air
optionB: Leave it in gear with the brake off
optionC: Apply the parking brake and switch off
optionD: Switch on the hazard warning lights only
explanation: Apply the parking brake, stop the engine, remove the key and lock the cab so the lorry cannot move or be taken.

question: What is the safest way to climb down from the cab?
optionA: Jump down from the top step quickly
optionB: Step down facing away from the cab
optionC: Use the door as a handhold
optionD: Face in, using steps and handles
explanation: Many drivers are injured jumping from cabs. Face in and use the steps and grab handles, keeping three points of contact.

question: Why should you check your mirrors before opening the cab door?
optionB: To see if the load has moved
explanation: A cyclist or motorcyclist could be passing close to the cab, so check before you open the door.

question: You are returning to the UK with a load. Why must you check the vehicle and keep it secure?
optionB: To stop people hiding on board
optionD: To pass the ferry's weight check
explanation: Operators and drivers can face civil penalties if clandestine entrants are found hidden in the vehicle, so check it and keep it locked.

question: Where is the safest place to park your loaded lorry overnight?
optionB: A lay-by on a main road
explanation: Secure, lit lorry parks reduce the risk of load and fuel theft and of people getting into the vehicle.

question: Without police permission, where must a lorry over 7.5 tonnes not be parked?
optionA: In a lay-by on a trunk road
explanation: Vehicles over 7.5 tonnes must not park on a verge, pavement or land between carriageways unless loading or unloading, and then not unattended.

question: You park a lorry at night on a road with a 40 mph limit. What must you do?
explanation: All vehicles must show parking lights when parked on a road or lay-by where the limit is over 30 mph.

question: You are parked on a public road, waiting several minutes to unload. What should you do?
optionA: Keep the engine idling to stay warm
optionB: Apply the parking brake and switch off
optionC: Rev the engine now and then
optionD: Keep it running to hold the air pressure
explanation: You must not leave an engine running unnecessarily while stationary on a public road. Idling wastes fuel and pollutes.

question: What is block changing?
optionC: Skipping gears when it is safe
explanation: Missing out intermediate gears, up or down, cuts gear changes and fuel use when the speed and load allow it.

question: Where on the rev counter should you keep the engine for the best fuel economy?
explanation: The green band is the most economical engine speed range. Changing up early within it saves fuel.

question: What is AdBlue used for in a modern diesel lorry?
explanation: AdBlue is injected into the exhaust where the SCR system uses it to cut nitrogen oxides. It never goes in the fuel tank.

question: What do air deflectors on a lorry cab help to do?
explanation: Correctly adjusted deflectors smooth airflow over the body, cutting wind resistance and fuel use.

question: How can planning your route help the environment?
optionA: It lets you drive faster on motorways
optionB: It means you can skip your breaks
optionC: It avoids congestion and wasted miles
explanation: A well-planned route cuts time stuck in traffic and wrong turns, saving fuel and emissions.

question: When is cruise control most likely to save fuel?
optionC: In thick fog on a busy motorway
optionD: On a clear, fairly level road
explanation: Cruise control keeps a steady speed and saves fuel on clear, level roads. In heavy traffic or poor conditions you need full control.

question: You break down on an ordinary road. How far behind the lorry should you place a warning triangle?
explanation: Put the triangle at least 45 metres behind on the same side of the road, using hazard lights too if you are causing an obstruction.

question: You break down on a motorway. Where should you place your warning triangle?
optionB: Do not use one on a motorway
explanation: Never use a warning triangle on a motorway; walking back along it is too dangerous. Use hazard lights and get to safety.

question: Your lorry breaks down on the motorway and you stop on the hard shoulder. Where should you wait?
optionA: In the cab with the doors locked
optionB: In front of the lorry on the verge
optionD: Beside the lorry on the hard shoulder
explanation: Get out on the side away from traffic if safe and wait well away from the vehicle, behind a barrier if there is one.

question: You break down in a live lane and cannot get out safely. What should you do?
optionA: Get out and push the lorry clear
optionB: Walk back to warn other traffic
optionC: Wait quietly for a patrol to pass
optionD: Keep your belt on and call 999
explanation: If you cannot get out safely, keep your seat belt on, switch on hazard lights and call 999.

question: On a motorway with no hard shoulder, where should you stop if your lorry develops a problem?
explanation: Leave at the next exit or stop in an emergency area. If you cannot reach one, move left if you can, use hazard lights and call 999.

question: A lorry in a crash shows plain orange reflective plates. What does this tell you?
optionC: It is wider than the normal limit
explanation: Plain orange plates mark packaged dangerous goods. Keep well away and give the emergency services as much detail as you can.

question: You arrive at an incident involving a tanker with hazard warning plates. What should you do?
optionA: Move closer to read the labels
optionB: Wait beside it for the fire service
optionC: Keep back and report the plates
explanation: Switch off engines, do not smoke, keep well away and give the details on the plates and labels when you call 999.

question: You are first to arrive at a crash. What should you do first?
optionB: Clear the debris from the road
optionC: Leave, as others will stop to help
optionD: Stop safely and use hazard lights
explanation: Protect the scene first: stop in a place of relative safety and use hazard lights, then call 999 with the location and casualty details.

question: When should you move someone injured in a crash?
optionA: Only if they are in immediate danger
optionB: As soon as you reach them
optionC: Once they say they feel well enough
optionD: Whenever you think it is safe to do so
explanation: Do not move casualties unless they are in immediate danger, for example from fire. Moving them can make injuries worse.

question: An injured motorcyclist is lying in the road. What should you not do?
optionA: Talk to them calmly and reassure them
explanation: Do not remove a motorcyclist's helmet unless it is essential, for example to keep their airway open.

question: How long should you cool a burn with clean, cool water?
explanation: The Highway Code advises cooling a burn for at least 20 minutes with plenty of clean, cool water.

question: When giving CPR to an adult, how deep should chest compressions be?
explanation: Press down hard and fast, about 5 to 6 centimetres, at about twice a second, in the centre of the chest.

question: A casualty is bleeding from a wound with nothing embedded in it. What should you do?
optionA: Apply firm pressure over the wound
optionB: Give them a hot, sweet drink to sip
optionD: Wash it out with cold running water
explanation: Firm pressure over the wound helps stem the bleeding. If something is embedded, press around it instead.

question: A casualty is unconscious but breathing. How should you position them?
explanation: Place an unconscious, breathing casualty in the recovery position until help arrives, keeping the airway open.

question: You hit a parked car and cannot find the owner. Within how long must you report it to the police?
explanation: If you do not give your details at the scene, you must report the collision to the police as soon as possible and within 24 hours.

question: Smoke starts coming from under your cab while driving. What should you do?
optionA: Tilt the cab to find where it comes from
optionB: Drive on to the next garage
optionC: Open the windows and carry on
optionD: Stop safely and switch off the engine
explanation: Pull over, switch off, get out and call 999. Do not tilt the cab or open panels, as more air can feed the fire.

question: Your brakes begin to fade on a long, steep hill. What may be provided to help you?
explanation: Escape lanes on steep descents let a runaway vehicle leave the road and stop in deep gravel or a slope.

question: Your lorry stalls on a level crossing. What should you do first?
optionA: Try to restart it several times
optionC: Walk along the line to warn the train
optionD: Push the lorry off the crossing
explanation: Get everyone out and clear first, then use the railway telephone to tell the signal operator. Move the vehicle only if there is time.

question: A fire starts in your lorry in a tunnel and you cannot drive out. What should you do?
optionA: Stay in the cab with the doors shut
optionB: Reverse back out to the tunnel entrance
optionC: Switch off, leave the key, get out
optionD: Open the bonnet to tackle it
explanation: Pull over, switch off the engine, leave the key in it and get out, using an emergency exit or refuge, then call for help.

question: Your trailer starts to snake as you drive downhill. What should you do?
optionA: Brake hard at once to slow down
explanation: Ease off gently and let the speed fall until the swaying stops. Harsh braking or steering can cause a jack-knife.

question: A circular sign with a red border shows a black lorry and "7.5T" below it. What does it mean?
optionB: Lorries over 7.5 tonnes use left lane
optionD: Parking for lorries up to 7.5 tonnes
explanation: Red circles give orders. This one bans goods vehicles over the maximum gross weight shown, often to keep lorries out of a town or estate.

question: A circular sign with a red border shows "18T" and no symbol. What does it mean?
optionD: Axle limit for lorries of 18 tonnes
explanation: A plain weight figure in a red circle is a weight limit for all vehicles over the gross weight shown, often at a weak bridge.

question: A circular sign with a red border shows a height with arrowheads above and below it. What does it mean?
optionB: Height of the next bridge in metres
optionC: No vehicles over the height shown
explanation: This is an order: vehicles taller than the height shown must not pass. Know your vehicle's height before you set off.

question: A circular sign with a red border shows a width with arrowheads either side of it. What does it mean?
optionA: Road narrows on both sides ahead
optionC: Width of the lane at the bridge
optionD: No vehicles over the width shown
explanation: Arrowheads at each side mean a width limit. Vehicles wider than the figure shown must not enter.

question: A red warning triangle shows a height figure between two black arrowheads. What does it warn of?
explanation: A triangle warns rather than orders: there is limited headroom ahead, such as a low bridge, at the height shown.

question: A red-ringed sign shows a lorry and "7.5T", with a plate below reading "Except for loading". What does it mean?
optionD: Lorries may park here while loading
explanation: The order bans goods vehicles over the weight shown, but the plate lets them in to load or unload there.

question: A direction sign shows a black lorry symbol beside one of the routes. What does this mean?
optionA: Lorries are banned on this route
explanation: A lorry symbol on a direction sign points goods vehicles to a route suited to them, avoiding low bridges and weak or narrow roads.

question: A red warning triangle shows a slope and "10%" with the road falling away. What does it warn of?
explanation: This warns of a steep descent. Select a low gear before the hill and use the endurance brake to avoid brake fade.

question: A red warning triangle shows a windsock blowing sideways. What does it warn of?
explanation: Side winds can push high-sided and lightly loaded lorries off course, especially on exposed bridges and open roads.

question: A red warning triangle shows a gate or barrier. What does it warn of?
optionA: A level crossing without a gate
optionC: A toll booth with a barrier
explanation: The gate symbol means the crossing has barriers or gates. A crossing without them is shown by a steam train symbol.

question: You see white posts with red diagonal stripes before a level crossing. What are they?
optionA: Markers for a hidden emergency exit
explanation: Red-striped posts count down to a concealed level crossing. Blue and white ones count down to a motorway exit.

question: A motorway gantry shows 50 inside a red ring. What does this mean?
explanation: A speed in a red ring is a legal limit, even on an overhead signal. Signals without a red ring are advisory.

question: A red X shows above your lane on a motorway. What does it mean?
explanation: A red X means the lane is closed. You must not drive in it beyond the signal.

question: A blue circular sign shows a white "30". What does it mean?
explanation: Blue circles give positive orders. A speed in a blue circle is a minimum; a maximum is shown in a red circle.

question: A red warning triangle shows a humped road. What does it warn of?
explanation: A hump bridge limits your view and can ground long, low vehicles, so slow down and do not overtake.

question: A lane sign reads "Crawler lane". Who is the lane for?
optionC: Lorries waiting to load or unload
explanation: A crawler lane lets slow, heavy vehicles climb in their own lane so faster traffic can pass safely.

question: You see two short yellow marks across the kerb. What do they mean?
explanation: Double yellow kerb marks mean no loading at any time. A single mark means loading is restricted at the times on the plate.

question: You see one short yellow mark across the kerb. What does it mean?
explanation: A single kerb mark means loading is not allowed at the times shown on the nearby plate.

question: What do double red lines along the edge of a road mean?
explanation: Double red lines on a red route mean no stopping at any time, even to load or unload.

question: What does a yellow criss-cross pattern painted on a junction mean?
optionA: Lorries may wait here to turn
optionB: Give way to buses using the junction
optionD: Enter only if your exit is clear
explanation: This is a box junction. Do not enter unless your exit is clear, except to wait to turn right behind oncoming traffic.

question: Long white lines in the middle of the road are continuous on your side. What does this mean?
optionA: Do not cross or straddle them
optionC: You may cross if the road is clear
explanation: You must not cross or straddle a continuous line on your side except to pass a stationary vehicle, to turn, or in the other exceptions allowed.

question: A red warning triangle shows a steam locomotive. What does it warn of?
explanation: The steam train symbol warns of a level crossing without barriers or gates, so look and listen before you cross.

question: A red circular sign shows a red car beside a black car. What does it mean?
explanation: This order means do not overtake from the sign onwards until it is lifted.

question: A red warning triangle shows two vertical arrows pointing in opposite directions. What does it warn of?
explanation: Opposing arrows in a triangle warn of two-way traffic ahead, for example where a one-way section or dual carriageway ends.
